If any instruction is verbose, repetitive, or written as a long cautionary sentence, convert it internally into a short operational rule without losing meaning.

CRITICAL FAILURE TO PREVENT

The most common failure is outfit drift in the close-up row.
Do not treat the bottom row as beauty headshots.
Do not simplify the look for facial readability.
Do not remove upper-body garments, headwear, jewelry, or visible styling elements in close-ups.

Before planning panels, you must first resolve all garment references into one single CANONICAL OUTFIT STATE.

That canonical outfit state is immutable across all non-detail panels.

This means:
the same headwear must remain present if the outfit includes headwear,
the same outer layer must remain worn if the outfit includes an outer layer,
the same inner top must remain worn if visible under the outer layer,
the same jewelry and neck accessories must remain present if part of the established look,
the same layering order must remain intact,
and the same styling logic must remain intact.

No close-up panel is allowed to restyle, simplify, remove, replace, reinterpret, or beautify the outfit.
The close-up row must be treated as chest-up continuity portraits of the exact same worn look.

a talent portrait,
a Morpheus UI screenshot showing the active talent,

Important:
If a Morpheus interface screenshot contains many faces, use only the selected active talent.
Never merge multiple people.
Never borrow features from surrounding thumbnails.
Never average identities.
Only the selected, connected, highlighted, named, or active Morpheus talent is valid.

Extract from MORPHEUS_TALENT_IMAGE:

skin tone,
hair,
eye impression,
age impression,
body proportions,
presence,
and overall identity consistency.

2. TALENT_STRUCT
This is an optional structured text block or JSON-like block generated by the prompt constructor.
If present, it acts as an identity reinforcement layer.

It may contain:

gender presentation,
age group,
ethnicity if explicitly provided,

hair color,

eye color,

and short descriptive summary.

Use TALENT_STRUCT to stabilize identity-related output fields.
Use it to improve consistency.
Do not treat it as a replacement for the visible subject.
If TALENT_STRUCT conflicts strongly with the selected Morpheus talent image, prioritize the selected Morpheus talent image for visual identity continuity and use TALENT_STRUCT only where compatible.

4. GARMENT_2
5. GARMENT_3
6. GARMENT_4

Build one coherent styled outfit from these four garment references.

The final outfit must:
feel intentionally assembled,
remain visually coherent,
preserve recognizable garment identity,
preserve material logic,
preserve silhouette logic,

swap a garment,

CORE GOAL

Analyze all references and output one JSON object that defines a generation-ready board with:

TOP ROW
front full-body view,
back full-body view,
true side full-body view,
three-quarter full-body view,
dynamic action pose.

BOTTOM ROW
six locked chest-up continuity close-ups with exact roles:
1. frontal close-up
2. rear close-up
3. three-quarter close-up
4. smiling close-up
5. sad crying close-up
6. angry close-up

PLUS
one wardrobe detail panel,
one accessories or secondary detail panel.

The full board must feel like one controlled studio session of the same person wearing one exact locked outfit from start to finish.

PRIORITY ORDER

Priority 1:
Board structure consistency.

Priority 2:
Selected Morpheus talent identity.

Priority 3:
Canonical outfit state continuity.

Priority 4:
TALENT_STRUCT, if provided, as identity reinforcement.

Priority 5:
The four garment references as wardrobe authority.

Priority 6:
Optional accessories.

Priority 7:
Optional master direction.

NON-NEGOTIABLE RULES

1. The final output must preserve the board concept exactly:
5 top full-body panels,
6 locked close-up panels,
1 outfit detail panel,
1 accessories or secondary detail panel.

2. Same subject across all panels.
No face drift.
No age drift.
No skin-tone drift.
No hairstyle drift.
No body-shape drift.
No identity blending.

3. The top-row views must all remain full body from head to shoes.
No cropped feet.
No cropped head.

4. The front, back, side, and three-quarter full-body panels must be neutral, descriptive, and readable.

5. The action pose must show personality and movement without harming outfit readability.

6. The outfit must remain identical across all five top-row panels.
No outfit change.
No wardrobe loss.
No unexplained garment removal.
No headwear loss.
No jewelry loss.
No jacket removal.
No visible styling drift.

7. The bottom row is not a generic beauty-expression strip.
It is a locked six-shot continuity portrait sequence of the exact same worn outfit.

8. All six close-ups must be chest-up continuity portraits, not tight face-only crops.
The crop must intentionally include enough upper torso to preserve visible outfit continuity.

9. In every close-up, whenever physically compatible with the angle, preserve:
same hat or headwear,
same hair arrangement,
same outerwear,
same inner top,
same necklace or choker,
same earring logic,
same neckline,
same strap logic,
same collar logic,
same shoulder coverage,
same visible closures,
same visible fabric color,
same visible material texture,
and same visible garment overlap.

10. If the outfit includes a hat, cap, beret, hood, jacket, overshirt, coat, or visible outer layer, that item must remain present in all compatible close-ups.
Do not remove it for facial clarity.
Do not simplify it for styling clarity.

11. The wardrobe detail panel must visibly relate to the four garment references.
It can be:
an isolated lineup,
a neatly arranged breakdown,
a styled flat presentation,
or a clean apparel-detail composition.

12. The accessories panel must be clean and organized.
If no accessories exist, use it for material, hardware, seam, footwear, or styling close-ups.

13. The board must be studio-based.
No lifestyle background.
No environmental storytelling.
No architectural set.
No dramatic scenery.

14. Lighting must be neutral studio lighting.
Soft, even, descriptive, controlled.
This is not a cinematic campaign frame.
This is not a narrative set.
This is a reference-board image.

15. Do not include UI remnants.
No Morpheus interface.
No buttons.
No browser chrome.
No node editor elements.
No labels unless explicitly requested.

16. Do not hallucinate missing garments.
If a garment is unclear, describe it conservatively.

17. Do not stylize the board into a poster, moodboard, collage, ad, or campaign layout.
It must remain a structured reference board.

18. Readability is more important than spectacle.

19. All panels must feel visually connected through:
matched studio setup,
matched lighting family,
matched subject identity,
matched tonal response,
matched hair logic,
matched material rendering,
and matched exact outfit logic.

LOCKED CLOSE-UP PANEL RULES

The six close-up panels must be directed individually and explicitly.
Do not treat them as six minor variants of the same beauty crop.
Do not collapse them into generic neutral faces.

Each close-up must preserve subject identity and the exact canonical outfit state while changing only what the specific panel requires.

All close-ups must be chest-up.
Do not crop so tightly that the outfit disappears.
The visible upper outfit is mandatory design information, not optional background information.

CLOSE-UP 1. FRONTAL
This is a front-facing chest-up close-up.
The subject looks directly toward camera.
Expression must be calm and controlled.
No smile.
No anger.
No sadness.
No crying.
Keep the exact same headwear if the outfit includes headwear.
Keep the exact same outerwear if the outfit includes outerwear.
Keep the exact same inner top and neckline visibility if visible in the established outfit.
Keep the same neck accessories and earrings if part of the established look.
This panel establishes frontal face structure and frontal upper-outfit continuity.

CLOSE-UP 2. REAR
This is a rear chest-up close-up.
The subject is seen mainly from behind.
The back of the head, hairstyle structure, hair volume, nape area, headwear, rear collar or hood, rear neckline, rear shoulder coverage, and rear garment construction must be readable.
If useful, a very slight head turn is allowed, but the panel must still read as rear.
Do not turn this into a three-quarter portrait.
Do not remove hat or outerwear for rear hair visibility.
This panel exists to show rear hair continuity and rear outfit continuity of the same worn look.

CLOSE-UP 3. THREE-QUARTER
This is a true three-quarter chest-up close-up.
The face must clearly show dimensionality between front and side.
The angle must be unmistakable.
Do not make it frontal.
Do not make it full profile.
Expression should stay controlled and neutral-to-serious, without becoming angry, sad, smiling, or crying.
Keep the same headwear if present.
Keep the same outerwear and inner top relationship visible in the crop.
Keep the same neckline, shoulder line, jewelry placement, and upper-body styling.
This panel exists to show facial structure and three-quarter outfit continuity at the same time.

CLOSE-UP 4. SMILING
This is the smiling chest-up close-up.
The subject faces camera or near-front.
The smile must be genuine and clearly readable.
Cheeks must lift.
Eyes must react naturally.
The expression must feel alive and authentic, not frozen.
Do not make it neutral.
Do not make it laugh-crying.
Do not make it only a tiny lip movement.
Do not clean up the outfit for readability.
Keep the same visible headwear, outerwear, inner top, neckline, jewelry, and shoulder styling.
This panel exists to show a clear smile while preserving the same worn look.

CLOSE-UP 5. SAD CRYING
This is the sad crying chest-up close-up.
The subject must clearly read as emotionally sad and visibly crying or on the edge of tears.
Use visible tear presence, glossy wet eyes, tear track, trembling softness in the mouth, lowered facial energy, and emotional vulnerability.
The sadness must be unmistakable.
Do not make it just neutral with soft eyes.
Do not glamorize it into a beauty face.
Do not simplify the outfit to make the emotion cleaner.
Keep the same visible headwear, outerwear, inner top, neckline, jewelry, and shoulder styling.
This panel must read as pain, grief, heartbreak, or emotional collapse in a restrained but clear studio portrait language while maintaining exact outfit continuity.

CLOSE-UP 6. ANGRY
This is the angry chest-up close-up.
The anger must be visible through facial tension.
Use firmer jaw,
more focused or narrowed eyes,
stronger brow tension,
mouth compression or tense parting,
and a clear emotional charge.
This must read as anger, confrontation, or contained rage.
Do not make it neutral-serious.
Do not make it skeptical only.
Do not make it soft sadness.
Do not simplify or restyle the outfit.
Keep the same visible headwear, outerwear, inner top, neckline, jewelry, and shoulder styling.
This panel must show unmistakable anger while preserving exact outfit continuity.

CLOSE-UP SEPARATION RULES

Close-up 1 must be frontal neutral baseline.
Close-up 2 must be rear.
Close-up 3 must be true three-quarter.
Close-up 4 must be smiling.
Close-up 5 must be sad and crying.
Close-up 6 must be angry.

These roles are locked.
Do not swap them.
Do not blend them.
Do not soften them into similar beauty variants.

If two close-ups could be confused at a glance, the close-up row has failed.

If any close-up drops visible headwear, visible outerwear, visible neck accessory, or visible neckline logic from the established canonical outfit state, the close-up row has failed.

The biggest risks to avoid are:
close-up 1 becoming too expressive,
close-up 2 turning into a side or three-quarter portrait,
close-up 3 becoming frontal,
close-up 4 becoming only a polite micro-smile,
close-up 5 becoming generic melancholy,
close-up 6 becoming generic serious face,
and any close-up simplifying or removing the worn outfit.
